metaData.originalTitle: An Oregon Law Lets One Wealthy Region Turn the Desert Green. When Drought Hits， Farmers Pay the Price.
metaData.title: An Oregon Law Lets One Wealthy Region Turn the Desert Green. When Drought Hits， Farmers Pay the Price.
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This investigation reveals how Oregon's century-old water rights law allows a wealthy irrigation district to waste vast amounts of water on grass and luxury estates while downstream farmers suffer crippling shortages during drought.
metaData.summary: ProPublica and Oregon Public Broadcasting analyze satellite data and state records to expose the inequities of Oregon's water allocation system. The Deschutes River is heavily diverted by the Central Oregon Irrigation District (COID), which holds senior water rights from the early 1900s. During a historic drought, only 26% of the diverted water was consumed by crops—mostly grass and pasture—while the rest leaked, evaporated, or ran off. Meanwhile, downstream farmers like Chris Casad in Jefferson County were forced to fallow fields and face financial ruin. The article traces the legal doctrine of 'beneficial use' and 'waste,' showing how loosely defined terms allow wealthy landowners—including Phil Knight's horse ranch and a luxury estate sold for $4.8 million—to maintain green lawns and low-value crops. The state has rarely canceled water rights, and COID actively monitors to ensure landowners use water at least once every five years to avoid losing rights. The report combines data visualizations, historical context, personal stories, and expert interviews to argue that the system prioritizes property rights over ecological health and economic fairness.

mainPoints.point: Senior water rights legally entitle COID to divert over half the Deschutes River during drought.
mainPoints.explanation: Oregon's 'first in time, first in right' system protects COID's allocation, forcing downstream farmers with junior rights to lose their water.

mainPoints.point: Only one of every four gallons COID takes is absorbed by crops; most is wasted.
mainPoints.explanation: Satellite data shows 45% of diverted water is lost in canals and 29% percolates or evaporates after delivery, leaving just 26% for crop consumption, almost entirely grass and pasture.

mainPoints.point: The legal definition of 'beneficial use' is so broad that growing any non-native crop qualifies.
mainPoints.explanation: Oregon courts rarely find waste, allowing landowners to irrigate aesthetic lawns and luxury landscapes without consequence.

mainPoints.point: The 'use it or lose it' rule incentivizes overconsumption to retain water rights.
mainPoints.explanation: COID actively patrols for unused land and sends letters warning landowners to keep irrigating, or risk cancellation of their water rights.

mainPoints.point: Downstream farmers and ecosystems bear the cost of this inequitable system.
mainPoints.explanation: While COID landowners enjoy abundant water, farmers like Chris Casad fallowed fields, and fish habitats suffer from reduced river flows of about 50% below ecological targets.

keyQuotes: At the same time, a few miles upstream, state law encouraged landowners to soak some of Oregon's most expensive real estate and least productive farmland, a ProPublica and Oregon Public Broadcasting analysis of water use has found.

relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe campaigns against out-of-state special interests funding ballot initiatives, yet his own tax-cutting measure benefits from undisclosed dark money from a Delaware nonprofit.

relatedArticles.title: “Digital Colonialism”: U.S. Demands to Access Africans’ Data Raise Privacy， Sovereignty Concerns
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This ProPublica investigation reveals how the Trump administration is conditioning lifesaving health aid to African nations on access to their citizens' sensitive health data, raising alarms about digital colonialism, privacy violations, and sovereignty.

relatedArticles.title: On the trail of the dotcom queen: how Julie Meyer left a pattern of unpaid bills， missing funds and broken dreams in her wake
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A Guardian investigation reveals that Julie Meyer, the celebrated 'dotcom queen' of First Tuesday fame, has left a trail of unpaid bills, missing funds, and broken dreams across multiple countries, with numerous allegations of fraud and manipulation.

relatedArticles.title: Trump Plans to Protect Methane-Leaking Stripper Wells. This Billionaire Donor Will Benefit.
